grammar.title: Zero and first conditional
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Zero conditional** → fatos, verdades gerais, coisas que **sempre** acontecem:
**If + present simple, present simple**
- "If you **heat** water to 100°C, it **boils**."
- "If I **drink** coffee after 6 p.m., I **can't** sleep."
(Aqui, **if** = **when**: sempre que.)

**First conditional** → situações **reais e possíveis no futuro** e suas consequências:
**If + present simple, will + verbo**
- "If it **rains** tomorrow, we**'ll stay** home."
- "If you **don't hurry**, you**'ll miss** the bus."
- "What **will** you **do** if you **don't get** the job?"

⚠️ **Regra de ouro:** depois de **if**, **nunca** use will: ❌ "If it will rain..." ✅ "If it **rains**..." (em português usamos o futuro do subjuntivo — "se chover" — mas em inglês é presente simples).

A ordem pode inverter (sem vírgula): "We'll stay home **if** it rains."

**Variações comuns na segunda parte:**
- modal: "If you finish early, you **can** go home." / "If it's sunny, we **might** go to the beach."
- imperativo: "If you see Ana, **tell** her to call me."
- going to: "If he's late again, I**'m going to** talk to him."

pronunciation.tip_pt: Na frase condicional, a voz **sobe** no fim da parte com if e **desce** no fim da consequência: "If it rains ↗, we'll stay home ↘." O **'ll** é rápido: "we'll" = "uíl", "you'll" = "iúl", "it'll" = "íról".

reading.title: Small habits, big results
reading.text: If you read ten pages a day, you'll read about a dozen books a year. If you save ten reais a day, you'll have more than 3,600 reais in twelve months. This is the logic behind "small habits", an idea popularized by writers like James Clear. The concept is simple: small actions, repeated consistently, produce big results over time. It works the other way too: if you sleep one hour less every night, you'll lose more than 300 hours of sleep in a year — and your health will suffer. Experts suggest using "if-then" plans to build new habits: "If it's 7 a.m., I'll drink a glass of water." "If I feel like checking social media, I'll do five push-ups first." Studies show that people who make if-then plans are much more likely to achieve their goals.

grammar.title: Second conditional + I wish
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Second conditional** → situações **imaginárias, hipotéticas ou improváveis** (no presente ou futuro):
**If + past simple, would + verbo**
- "If I **won** the lottery, I**'d buy** a house in the mountains."
- "If I **had** more time, I**'d learn** to play the guitar."
- "What **would** you **do** if you **lost** your job?"

O passado aqui **não fala do passado** — ele mostra **distância da realidade** (como o "se eu ganhasse" do português).

**If I were...** → com o verbo to be, use **were** para todas as pessoas (formal e recomendado): "If I **were** rich..." / "If she **were** here..." (Na fala informal, "if I was" também aparece.)

**Could / might** também funcionam: "If I had a car, I **could** visit you more often."

**First x second:**
- "If it **rains** tomorrow, I**'ll** stay home." → possível, realista
- "If it **snowed** in Rio, I**'d** build a snowman." → imaginário, improvável

**I wish + past simple** → desejo de que o **presente** fosse diferente:
- "I **wish** I **lived** near the beach." (mas não moro)
- "I **wish** I **were** taller."
- "I **wish** I **could** speak Japanese." (habilidade → could)

grammar.tip_pt: O **'d** pode ser **would** ou **had**. No second conditional, a parte com **'d** é sempre **would** + verbo base: "I'd travel" = I would travel.

pronunciation.tip_pt: **I'd** = "áid", **you'd** = "iúd", **we'd** = "uíd" — o D é curto, mas não pode sumir ("I travel" ≠ "I'd travel"). **Wouldn't** = "uúdent" (L mudo, T leve).

reading.title: Would money make you happier?
reading.text: If you suddenly became a millionaire, would you be happier? Most people say yes immediately. But research on lottery winners shows a more complicated picture. In a famous study from the 1970s, psychologists compared lottery winners with ordinary people and found that, after some time, the winners weren't much happier — they had adapted to their new lives. More recent research suggests that money does increase happiness, especially when it removes financial stress. But how you use it matters. People who spend money on experiences, on other people, or on buying time — like paying someone to do the chores they hate — tend to report more satisfaction than those who buy expensive things. So, if you won the lottery tomorrow, what would make you happier: a sports car, or more time with the people you love?

grammar.title: Unless e time clauses no futuro
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Unless** = **if... not** (a menos que):
- "**Unless** you study, you'll fail." = "**If** you **don't** study, you'll fail."
- ⚠️ Unless já é negativo: ❌ "Unless you don't study..."

**Time clauses no futuro** — a mesma regra do if: depois de **when, as soon as, before, after, until**, use o **presente simples**, mesmo falando do futuro:
- "I'll call you **when** I **arrive**." (❌ when I will arrive)
- "**As soon as** I **get** the results, I'll let you know."
- "We'll wait **until** the rain **stops**."
- "**Before** you **leave**, turn off the lights."
- "**After** I **finish** this course, I'm going to take the TOEFL."

Também dá para usar o **present perfect** para enfatizar que a ação estará completa: "I'll call you **as soon as** I**'ve finished**."

**In case** = por precaução (caso aconteça):
- "Take an umbrella **in case** it rains." (leve — talvez chova)
- Compare: "Take an umbrella **if** it rains." (só leve se estiver chovendo)

**As long as / provided that** = desde que (condição):
- "You can use my car **as long as** you **drive** carefully."

reading.title: SMART goals
reading.text: "I want to improve my English" is a wish, not a goal. Unless a goal is specific, it's very hard to achieve. That's why many coaches recommend SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Compare "I'll study more" with "I'll study English for 30 minutes a day, five days a week, until I reach B2 by December." The second one tells you exactly what to do, how to measure it and when the deadline is. Experts also suggest breaking big goals into milestones. As soon as you reach one, celebrate — and then move to the next. Keep track of your progress in a notebook or app, in case you lose motivation on difficult days: looking back at how far you've come is one of the best ways to keep going.

grammar.title: Revisão do B1 + estratégias de conversação
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Mapa do B1 — o que você já sabe:**
- **Tag questions:** It's nice, isn't it?
- **Present perfect:** experiências (Have you ever...?), duração (for/since), recentes (already/yet/just), continuous (I've been working...)
- **Modais:** can/could/be able to, could you...?, should/had better, must/have to/mustn't/don't have to, might/must be
- **Causative:** I got my hair cut.
- **Preferências:** I'd rather... / I prefer A to B
- **Verb patterns:** enjoy doing, decide to do, good at doing
- **Perguntas:** Who called? / Who did you call? / Do you know where...?
- **Passiva:** It was built in... / It is said that...
- **Narrativa:** past continuous + simple past + past perfect
- **Condicionais:** zero, first, second + unless, as soon as, I wish

**Estratégias de fluência** (o que nativos fazem o tempo todo):
1. **Ganhar tempo:** "Well...", "Let me think...", "That's a good question."
2. **Contornar palavras que faltam (paraphrasing):** "It's a kind of... / It's something you use to... / It's like..."
3. **Pedir esclarecimento:** "What do you mean by...?", "Could you rephrase that?"
4. **Desenvolver respostas** com a fórmula **A-R-E**: **A**nswer (resposta) → **R**eason (motivo) → **E**xample (exemplo).
   "Would you live abroad? — **Yes, I would.** **Because I love learning about other cultures.** **For example, when I visited Chile, I...**"
5. **Devolver a pergunta:** "What about you?"

It's a kind of... / It's something you use to... / It's like...
What do you mean by...? / Could you rephrase that?
For example... / For instance... / Like when I...
On the one hand... on the other hand... / However...
So, to sum up... / Anyway, that's what I think.

grammar.tip_pt: Na conversa, **fluência** (continuar falando) é mais importante que **precisão** (não errar nada). Nativos também erram, hesitam e se corrigem. Se travar, use uma estratégia em vez de parar ou mudar para o português!

common_mistakes.why_pt: Continue em inglês: peça ajuda ou descreva a palavra.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Conversa é troca. Devolver perguntas mostra interesse.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Falar rápido não é falar bem. Use **pausas** curtas entre ideias e **enfatize** as palavras-chave. Hesitações naturais em inglês são "um", "uh", "well", "you know" — não "é...", "tipo..." em português!

reading.title: The intermediate plateau
reading.text: Many English learners feel fast progress at the beginning: every week, they can say new things. Then, around B1, something strange happens: progress seems to stop. This is known as the intermediate plateau. It happens because you can already communicate in most everyday situations, so you're no longer forced to learn new language. You keep using the same words and structures that "work". How can you break the plateau? Teachers suggest three things. First, consume more authentic content — podcasts, series, YouTube channels and articles about topics you love. Second, push yourself to use new vocabulary on purpose, even if you make mistakes. Third, get feedback: record yourself, write texts and ask someone to correct them. The plateau isn't a sign that you've stopped learning. It's a sign that you're ready for the next level.

questions.q: What is the intermediate plateau?
questions.answer: A period around B1 when progress seems to stop.

questions.q: Why does it happen?
questions.answer: You can already communicate, so you keep using the same words and structures.

questions.q: What are the three suggestions?
questions.answer: Consume authentic content, use new vocabulary on purpose, get feedback.

questions.q: What is the plateau a sign of, according to the text?
questions.answer: That you're ready for the next level.

writing.model: When I started learning English, I couldn't understand a single song, and I was terrified of speaking. I had tried to learn several times before, but I had always given up after a few months. This time was different. I've been studying for almost two years now, and I've learned much more than grammar. I've learned to stop translating everything in my head and to keep talking even when I make mistakes. The most difficult part was the present perfect — I still sometimes say "I live here since..."! I wish I had more time to study, but I'm proud of my progress. As soon as I finish this level, I'm going to start B1+. If everything goes well, I'll take an international exam next year. speaking_questions: Tell me about yourself and your English journey.
What's the most interesting experience you've ever had?
What would you change about your life if you could?
What are your goals for the next year? What will you do if things go wrong?
What advice would you give someone who is starting to learn English?
review.project_pt: **Projeto final B1 — "My TED-style talk":** prepare e grave uma mini-palestra de 3 a 4 minutos sobre um tema que você domina ou ama (sua profissão, um hobby, uma experiência que mudou sua vida). Estrutura: uma história pessoal (tempos narrativos), o que você aprendeu (present perfect), uma ideia para o público (should / if) e um convite final (imagine if...). Esse é o aquecimento para o B1+, que é todo baseado em TED Talks! 🎤
